name: openfst
why: Weighted finite-state transducers are a fascinating formal-language idea, though it is a library first.

brief.what_it_is: OpenFst is an open-source C++ template library for building, combining, optimizing, and searching weighted finite-state transducers (FSTs). Each transition in these automata has an input label, an output label, and a weight, and the finite-state acceptor is the special case where input and output labels match. The library takes FSTs as input, whether built in code or from AT&T-format text files, and produces new FSTs or search results such as shortest paths. It also ships about 60 shell commands (fstcompile, fstcompose, fstshortestpath, and others, plus far* and pdt/mpdt tools) that read and write binary FST files.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes FSTs as a way to represent sets of strings (acceptors) and binary relations between strings (transducers), with key uses in speech recognition and synthesis, machine translation, OCR, pattern matching, and information extraction. The library was developed by contributors from Google Research and NYU's Courant Institute and is meant to be comprehensive, reliable, flexible, efficient, and to scale well.
brief.how_it_works: Weights form a semiring: one operation (Plus) combines alternative paths with the same labels, and another (Times) combines weights along a path. Predefined weight types include Tropical and Log, which suit shortest-path and probabilistic models. Operations such as determinization, minimization, composition, and shortest path are applied to FSTs, which can be chained together. The shell commands read binary FST files, run the matching C++ operation, and write an output file, using standard input and output when file names are omitted.

commands_seen.context: Install route given on the homepage for Linux (x86) and Mac OS X users who already have conda.
Converts an AT&T-format text FST into a binary FST, mapping symbolic labels through the symbol table files.
Prints a summary of an FST: state and arc counts, initial and final states, and properties such as deterministic, acyclic, and weighted.
Prints a binary FST in text form using the symbol tables.
Writes a Graphviz dot drawing of an FST; the quick tour then renders it with dot -Tps.
Sorts arcs by output label, which composition needs on one of its two inputs.
Computes the relational composition of two transducers, here applying a model to an input.
Keeps only the output labels of a transducer, yielding an acceptor of output strings.

commands_seen.cmd: fstarcsort --sort_type=ilabel model.fst | fstcompose input.fst - | fstproject --project_output result.fst
commands_seen.context: Single-pipeline version of the sort, compose, and project steps, showing that the tools chain through stdin and stdout.

brief.install_notes: Installing from source is not covered on the pages I read; the homepage only gives the conda-forge command for Linux (x86) and Mac OS X. To use the C++ API, include <fst/fstlib.h> from the installation include directory and link against libfst.so in the library directory. The shell tools are in the installation bin directory, and --help gives usage for each. No accounts, hardware, or first-run configuration were mentioned.
brief.standout: Weighted transducers unify acceptors, transducers, and probabilistic models behind one semiring framework, so composition, determinization, and shortest path work the same way across speech, translation, and string-processing uses. The shell commands are small Unix-style filters that can be piped together, as the quick tour's one-line composition example shows.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage (a TWiki page last revised 2024-12-23) announces OpenFst version 1.8.4 as available and says it is now on conda-forge. I did not find a release date for 1.8.4 or a recent commit. The quick tour page was last edited in 2020.
brief.caveats: The primary interface is a C++ template library; the command-line tools are a secondary interface. The homepage and docs are on an old TWiki site, and I found no GitHub README. The quick tour I read was last edited in 2020, and one of its links returned 404 (FstQuickTour is the working URL). Licensing is Apache, per the homepage. The default arc type is StdArc, and the docs warn that a path with weight 0 is not allowed. I saw no build or platform warnings beyond the conda note.
quotes: OpenFst is a library for constructing, combining, optimizing, and searching weighted finite-state transducers (FSTs).
It is intended to be comprehensive, reliable, flexible, efficient, and to scale well.
As an alternative interface, there are shell-level commands in the installation bin directory that operate on file representations of FSTs.
